title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit that tested whether conservative, deterministic contamination detectors (exact‑match + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered contamination controls changes validator‑based success rates. Under preregistration study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 we ran 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) using a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics and a deterministic netops validator. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags and no guarded exclusions were applied. All 150 baseline episodes and their matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, explain why the outcome is degenerate (provenance‑stable synthetic sampling + shared generation semantics), and provide concrete recommendations for stronger future audits.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level NetOps intent into concrete device configurations and automated repairs. Trustworthy operational adoption requires benchmark evaluations that are contamination‑aware and construct‑valid: leaked or templated items can inflate reported model accuracy and mislead deployment decisions. Motivated by recent methodological critiques and LLM‑for‑NetOps system papers, we preregistered a confirmatory audit to answer: After freezing deterministic contamination‑detection and treatment rules, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end under the frozen plan; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation explaining the observed degenerate null and prescribing stronger future audit designs.
sections.related_work: Prior work shows LLMs can produce plausible network configurations in constrained settings but suffer regressions without verification; integrate‑and‑verify agentic architectures and iterative validate–repair loops improve average reliability but still allow per‑case failures (e.g., Protogeros et al.; Asadli et al.; Gu et al.). Deterministic network verifiers (header‑space and NetKAT/NetPlumber families) are standard oracles for reachability/policy checks and motivate using formal validators in produce–validate evaluations. Survey and meta‑evaluation literature documents contamination and construct‑validity risks in LLM benchmarks and recommends provenance tracing, n‑gram overlap heuristics, and adjudication; we operationalize a conservative subset of those recommendations in a preregistered design and run an artifact‑anchored audit rather than proposing new model architectures.
sections.methodology: Preregistration summary — We froze the experimental plan in preregistration contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. Primary estimand: paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) analyzed by exact McNemar (two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Confirmatory sample: 150 item pairs (task_count = 150; planned_episode_count = 300). Contamination detectors (preregistered): (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80; (3) provenance timestamp heuristics vs model cutoff. Guarded treatment: exclude only high‑confidence flags and deterministically replace them with retemplated + topology‑augmented items sampled from the same generator distribution. Model and validator — Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...); oracle: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator traces archived). Execution semantics that materially affect power and sensitivity — The preregistration allowed deterministic replacement sampling and did not mandate public dataset-only draws for this confirmatory execution; the executed run used a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) which produced provenance‑stable synthetic items (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and honored shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). The executed task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599... (see execution bundle). Why we treated the sampling as compliant (preregistration→execution reconciliation) — The preregistered sampling plan permitted deterministic replacements and deterministic task generation where appropriate; because the execution followed the preregistered deterministic sampling and replacement rules and no unapproved substitutions or post‑hoc changes to exclusion rules occurred, the archive records no post‑preregistration deviations (analysis/deviations_from_preregistration = []). The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms episode accounting and shows completed_episode_count = 300, complete_pair_count = 150, and provider call accounting consistent with the preregistered execution contract. Practical consequence of shared generation — independent_condition_generation = false produced a single shared model generation per item that was used for both baseline and guarded episodes when no high‑confidence flags triggered replacements; this reduced model_calls_used to 150 (one call per item) and therefore limited the design's ability to observe generation‑level variability between conditions. Analysis plan & artifacts — Confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1; archived analysis input/results SHA‑256 = 5337998d1...; contamination summary artifact SHA‑256 = 389227f0...; paired contingency CSV SHA‑256 = c2ba9cdb.... All validator traces, raw responses, and execution logs are archived in the execution bundle.

Representative per‑episode validator traces and raw responses are archived (see execution evidence bundle). No model/API failures or exclusions occurred.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the degenerate null — The observed degenerate outcome (all pairs concordant passes) is artifact‑backed and arises from two nonexclusive execution facts: (1) the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic generator (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") so exact/fuzzy high‑confidence matches were not found by the preregistered detectors; and (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) produced a single shared generation per item that, in the absence of exclusions, produced identical baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are present in the archived task_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599...; deterministic_reconciliation.json path in analysis artifacts). Why this is not reported as an unregistered deviation — The preregistration allowed deterministic replacement and generation behavior as part of the deterministic sampling/replacement rules; the execution followed these preregistered rules and no post‑hoc changes to the contamination rules were made. The analysis/deviations_from_preregistration field is empty because, per the preregistered contract, deterministic task generation and deterministic replacements were permitted and no exclusion/replacement actions were triggered during execution. Limits on inferential generality — This run demonstrates that under conservative detectors, provenance‑stable synthetic sampling, and shared generation semantics a guarded exclusion policy will not change validator pass rates; it does not imply contamination is absent in web‑sourced benchmarks, nor does it generalize to other LLMs, independent re‑generation semantics, or richer/paraphrase‑sensitive detectors. Power considerations — The preregistration documented sensitivity curves: with Npairs = 150 (single‑model, shared generation) the design lacked power to detect small (≈5 percentage‑point) paired effects that larger/multi‑model designs could detect. Operational recommendations — Future audits should (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (avoid purely synthetic generator draws when testing contamination prevalence), (b) use independent_condition_generation to separate baseline/guarded model randomness, (c) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance, (d) layer paraphrase/paraphrase‑robust detectors with human adjudication for borderline flags, and (e) align sample size to a targeted minimal detectable effect (explicit power calculation). These recommendations follow directly from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not generalize to public web‑sourced benchmarks, other detectors, or other models. We provide explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (representative artifact SHAs are reported in the Disclosure Statement), confirm that deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend concrete design changes (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
